DID (according to ICD11)
- distinct parts
- they can switch
- usually have full amnesia but not always

partial DID:
- distinct parts
- they can't switch (or only rarely/in high stress moments)
- usually have less amnesia than "classic" DID

OSDD1b:
- distinctive alters
- only partial/emotional amnesia mostly

Anxiety does not mean you’re failing, it means your system is trying to protect you. Storms pass. Cold eases.Support returns, power returns. If you’re finding this unbearable, reach out to local supports or crisis lines in your area. Help is part of preparedness too. #MentalHealth #Anxiety #Storm

Ice storms are tough because they’re invisible but dangerous. You can’t always see the risk. If you’re feeling anxious right now, go to familiar routines that work for you. Focus on your needs for the next 2 hrs. The nervous system calms with short, manageable steps. #MentalHealth #Anxiety #Storm

Major winter storms don’t just disrupt travel and power,they can seriously affect mental health. For people living with anxiety, uncertainty & loss of control can be overwhelming and can trigger anxiety,panic and more. These reactions are normal under threat. #MentalHealth #Anxiety #Storm

Wellbeing tips aren’t the problem in #MentalHealth. They become a problem when they’re presented as sufficient rather than supportive. So yes, small things can help a little with #Anxiety. But anxiety treatment deserves understanding, structure, and care. And pretending otherwise helps no one.

Real #Anxiety support needs a holistic approach:
• nervous system regulation
• psychological skills
• context and meaning
• compassion over pressure
• time
No hacks. No shortcuts. #MentalHealth #Davos
What I shared wasn’t treatment for #MentalHealth difficulties. It was light, situational advice , things that might take the edge off in the moment, not resolve the deeper system. #Anxiety #Davos

I got pulled up by a colleague for sharing four tips for people feeling anxious about #Davos and the so-called “new world order”. Fair enough, if it sounded like #Anxiety can be solved with a short list, that wasn’t my intent.

If stressed by the political world: you’re not weak or “overreacting.” Uncertainty makes the nervous system scan for threat. Tips: 1.Talk with a trusted person 2.do a small helpful thing this week 3.set news-feed boundaries 4.be kind to yourself. One breath, one step. #MentalHealth #Anxiety #Davos

In a more uncertain world, reassurance can feel hollow, and anxiety can turn into despair. Mental health support isn’t about saying “everything will be OK”, it’s about helping people stay engaged with life when nothing feels OK. #MentalHealth #Anxiety #Davos

Integrating psychological coping strategies into public health education and policy is essential, with interventions that are accessible, culturally responsive, and scalable.
#MentalHealth #Anxiety #climate

These approaches are especially important for vulnerable populations, where climate-related mental health impacts are often greatest and supports least accessible.
#MentalHealth #Anxiety #climate

Practices such as mindfulness, cognitive reframing, and environmental engagement can help transform climate anxiety into proactive, values-driven behaviour.
#MentalHealth #Anxiety #climate

Evidence highlights positive psychology as a promising approach to addressing climate-related mental health challenges by strengthening resilience and mental capacity.
#MentalHealth #Anxiety #climate

As the global impacts of climate change become more apparent, so do the psychological effects, climate anxiety, stress, helplessness, and hopelessness.
Mental health is now part of the climate conversation.
#MentalHealth #Anxiety #climate

text:
People are already using AI to cope. The question is no longer whether AI plays a role in emotional support, but how responsibly, safely and transparently it’s designed.
#MentalHealth #Anxiety

This is why science-based AI matters. Emotional support systems need grounding in evidence, clear boundaries, escalation pathways and an understanding of how anxiety actually works, not just good conversation. #MentalHealth #Anxiety

Unstructured emotional conversations + vulnerable users + systems optimised for fluency = a genuine risk of reinforcing anxiety, dependence or distorted thinking if guardrails aren’t built in. #MentalHealth #Anxiety
The real risk isn’t that people seek emotional support from AI. It’s that much of today’s AI was never designed with psychology, anxiety science, or safeguarding in mind. #MentalHealth #Anxiety

Most people aren’t using clinical tools. They’re turning to general-purpose AI because it’s available, responsive and non-judgemental. That tells us something important about unmet emotional needs.
#MentalHealth #Anxiety

A third of UK citizens have already used AI for emotional support. This isn’t speculative or niche, it’s happening now, at scale, because people are struggling and support is scarce.
#MentalHealth #Anxiety

Political anxiety feels different now. It’s not just what’s happening, but what’s real.
AI and misinformation demand constant vigilance. How do therapists and clients stay grounded in shared reality and safety together? It need more media literacy and care than ever.
#MentalHealth #Anxiety

Your point actually highlights an important truth: population mental health improves most when basic needs are met. Therapy works alongside material conditions, not instead of them. Thanks for calling that out.

The previous few posts were informed by reporting from CBC News, by Campbell MacDiarmid, Published March 7, 2025
on rising anxiety linked to the current political climate.
#MentalHealth #Anxiety

One important point: people feel relief simply knowing they’re not alone or “overreacting.” Shared reality and human connection remain core therapeutic tools.
#MentalHealth #Anxiety

Action, whether protest, values-based choices, or setting boundaries with news, can reduce helplessness. Therapy isn’t about disengaging from the world, but engaging with it more sustainably.
#MentalHealth #Anxiety

Political anxiety is showing up as sleep loss, anger, financial fear, and parenting stress.
Therapy increasingly needs to work with context, not just symptoms.
#MentalHealth #Anxiety

Therapists highlight an important shift: reassurance alone isn’t enough when external threats feel real. Validation and nervous-system support matter more than “everything will be fine.”
#MentalHealth #Anxiety

With every thing going on at the moment it’s worth remembering that when the world feels unstable, anxiety can be a reasonable response, not a cognitive error. Good therapy doesn’t dismiss that reality, it helps people regulate while staying grounded in it.
#MentalHealth #Anxiety

text:
Encouraging science. Early days.
But another reminder that anxiety is not a weakness, it’s a complex, multi-system process that works best when balance is restored. #MentalHealth #Anxiety
From an anxiety-science perspective, this aligns with a key principle: mental health isn’t about eliminating fear, it’s about strengthening the systems that regulate it. #MentalHealth #Anxiety

Crucially, when both microglial systems were present, anxiety stayed in check.
It wasn’t about removing anxiety entirely, but about restoring balance. #MentalHealth #Anxiety

The study suggests anxiety two competing populations of microglia (brain immune cells) act like an internal accelerator & brake on anxiety levels (in mice). Might explain why anxiety spirals when regulatory systems fail to counterbalance threat responses. #MentalHealth #Anxiety

Just finished reading a fascinating piece from University of Utah Health (27 Dec 2025) on new research into how brain immune cells may regulate anxiety published in Molecular Psychiatry. Posts to follow based on this.
#MentalHealth #Anxiety

The future isn’t magic mushrooms vs therapy. It’s understanding who, when, and under what conditions deeper interventions are safe. Hope matters. So does caution.
Mental health care works best when evidence, ethics, and human variability are held together, not rushed apart. #MentalHealth #Anxiety

Even if approved for NHS use, psychedelics could never be a stand-alone solution.
They could only work as an adjunct to structured psychological care. Innovation in mental health is welcome. But progress means precision, not hype, especially when anxiety is involved. #MentalHealth #Anxiety

Fast emotional change without regulation can overwhelm anxious brains, increasing avoidance rather than reducing it. This is why preparation, context, and integration matter more than the molecule itself.
The experience is not the treatment.
What happens after is. #MentalHealth #Anxiety
From a clinical perspective, this isn’t surprising. Psychedelics intensify perception, memory, and threat processing, systems already sensitive in anxiety disorders. #MentalHealth #Anxiety

The debate on psilocybin & depression often misses something vital: anxiety is at the core of both the benefits and the risks.
Psychedelics don’t just lift mood, they amplify emotional learning. #MentalHealth #Anxiety
This thread is inspired by a thoughtful article by Pallab Ghosh on the BBC website (2 Jan 2026) on the debate over psilocybin, depression, and the NHS. #MentalHealth #Anxiety

#MentalHealth #Anxiety #Stress

Anxiety, chronic stress, and emotional overload rarely trigger detention, until they escalate. These are not minor issues; they are the conditions that quietly push people toward crisis.

However, legislation also highlights a deeper truth: by the time someone is detained, the system has already failed upstream. Crisis reform is essential, but prevention is everything.

Reforming detention isn’t just legal housekeeping. It’s an ethical shift: care must be therapeutic, proportionate, and centred on the person, not administrative convenience.
#MentalHealth #Anxiety #Stress

Happy New Year to every mental health professional, every LFC fan, and every book lover. Thanks for being part of the journey. On we go into 2026.
#LFC #MentalHealth #Anxiety #Books

Note:
This thread was inspired by “Sorry Dante, middle age is not a road to Hell” by Oliver Moody, The Times (31.01.2025), and reflects on mental health, anxiety, and the realities of midlife through that lens.
#MentalHealth #Anxiety #Stress #Midlife

10.
Maybe midlife anxiety isn’t the opposite of mental health. Maybe it’s the cost of a brain doing the hardest work it will ever do: holding a life together.
#MentalHealth #Anxiety #Stress #Midlife

9.
Middle age isn’t where the self disappears. It’s where it stabilises, shaped by endurance, compromise, and responsibility. That process can feel anxious, but it’s meaningful.
#MentalHealth #Anxiety #Stress #Midlife

8.
We’re sold a myth that the “real self” is discovered in youth. In reality, selves are built (slowly) through relationships, care, and constraint.
#MentalHealth #Anxiety #Stress #Midlife

7.
Midlife anxiety often isn’t a mental health failure. It’s what happens when real responsibility meets a nervous system learning to carry it.
#MentalHealth #Anxiety #Stress #Midlife

6.
This is crystallised intelligence: the ability to navigate complexity, tolerate uncertainty, and make decisions under pressure are the exact skills midlife demands.
#MentalHealth #Anxiety #Stress #Midlife

5.
From our 30s onward, the brain builds dense local networks instead of chasing novelty. Less speed. More judgement, integration, and emotional regulation.
#MentalHealth #Anxiety #Stress #Midlife

4.
Neuroscience complicates the “midlife decline” story. The brain doesn’t stop developing, it reorganises.
#MentalHealth #Anxiety #Stress #Midlife

3.
This anxiety isn’t weakness. It’s the fear that one shock (illness, redundancy, family crisis) could destabilise a carefully balanced life.
#MentalHealth #Anxiety #Stress #Midlife

2.
For many, midlife means being part of the sandwich generation: supporting children and ageing parents while holding work, money, and identity together. Anxiety here isn’t occasional, it’s constant background noise. 
#MentalHealth #Anxiety #Stress #Midlife

Middle age is often painted as a grey slog, and the data backs it up. Life satisfaction drops after 30 by almost as much as divorce or job loss. No surprise anxiety rises. But that’s not the full story.
#MentalHealth #Anxiety #Stress #Midlife
Thank you for letting me know. Will try to fix it.
When we treat mental illness as a moral failing or a trend, we delay care and deepen suffering. Science, compassion, and functioning-focused support must lead. #MentalHealth #Anxiety

Another narrative suggests diagnosis is the problem. The problem is actually what happens after diagnosis. Too often, very little. We need care that addresses anxiety, stress, coping, and context, not culture-war narratives. #MentalHealth #Anxiety

We need to urgently debunk the narrative that rising mental health need is evidence of malingering. The growing need reflects real distress, social change, post-Covid disruption, and services that haven’t kept pace. Denial doesn’t reduce demand. Care does. #MentalHeslth #Anxiety

Regulator: “insufficient evidence” that personal therapy benefits trainees. O’Connor (Sunday Times Ireland) argues this logic ignores real-world clinical risk. Mental health regulation should protect patients. If it fails vulnerable people, it becomes part of the problem. #MentalHealth #Anxiety

Mandatory personal therapy is a global norm in psychotherapy training. According to professional bodies cited by O’Connor, removing it would leave Ireland with the lowest standards in Europe. Sunday Times Ireland. #MentalHealth #Anxiety

The most alarming proposal? Trainee therapists may no longer be required to undergo personal therapy themselves. That’s a serious safety issue. Sunday Times Ireland Alison O’Connor. #MentalHealth #Anxiety

As O’Connor writes, therapy has become more accepted and more available, but regulation is now heading in a troubling direction. Standards for training therapists are being weakened, not strengthened. #MentalHealth #Anxiety

People seeking help for anxiety or acute psychological distress assume their therapist is properly trained and regulated. That assumption may no longer hold.
Alison O’Connor, Sunday Times Ireland #MentalHealth #Anxiety

so far Cals is the pigs my friend and I had the most issues with and some of my other more professional friends have also stated that they tend to have severe losses with them too. 

I will focusing on my 2nd passion: Sheba guinea pigs instead and PERFECT Abbys
I may come back to them later once more advanced breeders can breed them out. For me due to my small apartment I sadly cannot help.

While the size and growth of this breed does way better than other pigs, they end up mysteriously getting sick often along with moms struggling to birth due to their size. Theyre still my favorite colors but this isn't good for the pigs health with is our main priority

My friends have also stopped due to this as pigs should be healthy. Sadly this also isn't the breeds fault entirely as too many US ones leads back one major line therefore too many issues arises. 

I will be focusing on other and more advanced breeds that are less new to avoid these issues.

Took a huge loss in our caviary tonight. The breed that Ive been ethically showing and breeding has been discovered to have too many health problems therefore I have decided to stop breeding them as it is against my ethical standards. A strong democracy depends on a well-informed public. 

That requires a media environment that prioritizes substance over spectacle.

Canadians deserve better—and we are capable of better.

When leaders are addressing the public on important issues, the expectation should be that questions remain relevant, constructive, and focused on informing citizens—not creating headlines or unnecessary division.
If our media appears unserious or driven by division, it risks undermining that confidence at a time when it matters most.

We in Canada should strive to be a model for how responsible journalism supports a strong and healthy democracy.

We are in a time when countries are looking to Canada—for trade, for cooperation, for stability.
Canada has the opportunity to set an example—to show that it is still possible to have a media environment that is fair, balanced, and focused on informing the public in a meaningful way.
This is not limited to one reporter, one outlet, or even one country—it is a broader trend all over the world. But I would hope that here in Canada, we can aim higher.

At a time when democracies are facing real pressure, including efforts by bad actors to sow division, media plays a critical role.

When reporting leans into conflict rather than clarity, it can unintentionally—or at times even deliberately—contribute to that division.

It weakens it.

This concern is not about supporting one party or criticizing another.
It is about standards.
It is about ensuring that journalism remains grounded in responsibility, professionalism, and a commitment to being unbiased—not driven by reaction, clicks or spectacle.

Instead, they risk pulling leaders into unnecessary conflict and shifting focus away from matters that actually affect people’s lives.

Asking questions that tap into outrage, or framing discussions in a way that demonizes political opponents—regardless of party—does not strengthen democracy.

What is the intention behind that question?

You can easily find numerous examples of this kind of unprofessional behaviour.

Questions like that do not clarify policy, explain decisions, or help citizens make sense of complex issues.

For example, I recently heard a reporter ask the Prime Minister of Canada whether he believed the leader of the opposition should resign following a majority result.

It raises a simple question: how does that inform Canadians? 
What value does that add to public understanding?

Increasingly, we’re seeing questions that are either poorly thought out or designed to elicit a negative or divisive response. 

This does not serve the public—it only distorts the conversation.

There is also a responsibility within the profession itself. Reporters should be held to account by their peers. 

Standards matter, and maintaining them should not fall solely on the public.

The goal was to inform—not to provoke, divide, or chase reaction. That standard feels like it’s slipping.

Leaders should absolutely be held to account, but it must be done in a professional manner. Reporters should act like professionals, not like high school students looking for a reaction.

On feet unsteady

Upwards to heights
Downward, begin again

embedded_title: Peter Raven, groundbreaking botanist, dies at 89
embedded_description: World-renowned botanist Peter Raven who turned a minor botanical garden in the U.S. heartland into an international research and conservation powerhouse, died at 89 years old on April 25, according to the Missouri Botanical Garden (MBG). In nearly four decades as president and director of the Missouri Botanical Garden in St. Louis, Raven raised the little-known arboretum to the status of a world-class institution, using it as a base for plant research throughout the Americas, Asia, Africa, and Madagascar. "He literally transformed public gardens into tools of outreach to help people understand the value of science in preserving biodiversity and the conservation of plants," said U.S. National Arboretum Director Colien Hefferan in awarding Raven her institution's Medal of Excellence in 2014. Influence and impact In 1999, Time magazine called Raven a "Hero for the Planet," and his influence as a researcher, mentor, and champion of conservation extended far beyond the Midwest. Generations of scientists count themselves part of "Raven's army," said botanist Pete Lowry, former director of the MBG's Africa and Madagascar department. "He was a connector of people. His impacts were multiple and multifaceted." Raven influenced and helped many researchers as a trustee and chair for nearly 15 years...

embedded_title: Study finds popular AI chatbots often give problematic health advice
embedded_description: A new audit suggests that widely used free AI chatbots can sound confident while delivering misleading health information, weak citations, and advice that may be unsafe without expert guidance. Study: Generative artificial intelligence-driven chatbots and medical misinformation: an accuracy, referencing and readability audit. Image Credit: Bankiras / Shutterstock In a recent study published in the journal BMJ Open, researchers audited the accuracy, referencing, and readability of five popular artificial intelligence (AI)-driven chatbots to investigate how they responded to health queries in misinformation-prone fields. The study utilized 250 prompts across five misinformation-prone categories, with outputs evaluated by two subject-matter experts in each category using predefined criteria. Study findings revealed that while aggregate performance did not differ significantly across models (p = 0.566), an alarming 49.6% of AI-generated responses were problematic or failed to align clearly with scientific consensus and appropriate framing. Furthermore, individual models demonstrated distinct behavioral vulnerabilities (e.g., poor reference authenticity and college-level readability scores), highlighting the urgent need for greater oversight and user caution when leveraging public-facing health AI technologies. What can we do? Counteract immediately and as often as possible. 

Be aware of your biases and invite others to be aware of theirs.

#biases #emotionalintelligence

11/12
Repetition bias: there is a willingness in most of us to believe what we have been told most often. If you hear often enough that a certain politician is crooked, you will automatically and unconsciously have a more negative view of them. Even if you had thought before that they were excellent

10/12
Backfire effect: when we attack people for having made wrong choices in the past, they will double down and defend their actions. Don’t attack others, just invite them to look at another possibility and offer them choice (don’t tell them what to do).

9/12
Sunk cost bias: we cling to things we have invested in.  If people have put years of energy in certain ideas, they will find it hard to let go. We need to offer them different ideas that lead in a more useful direction or pay them back for the time/energy/emotions invested.

8/12
Barnum effect: we see specifics in vague statements by filling in the gaps. “Make America great again” doesn’t mean anything, but people assigned meaning to it that they thought would be of benefit to them. Force candidates to be specific!

7/12
Framing effect: we are influenced by context and delivery of a message. That’s why candidates love to hang out with celebrities and display the flag at any possible opportunity. Read about their ideas and policies without any of the show around them.

6/12
Halo/Horns effect: we tend to take one good or bad thing about a candidate and generalise it. That’s why it is so easy to act like someone who has done a bad thing once is a bad person and another who has done a good thing is a good person forever. Check for consistency!

5/12
Optimism bias: we tend to believe the people who make the most optimistic promises and who tell us that we don’t have to listen to those who say that there might be pain ahead. Positive thinking is a good start, but a bad strategy.

4/12
Overconfidence bias: an expert in one field is not necessarily (and maybe not even likely) an expert in an unrelated field. A good hairdresser is not necessarily a good cook. A good sports figure/entertainer/celebrity is not necessarily a good or effective politician.

3/12
Certainty bias: we tend to want to follow people who sound like they know what they’re doing. But most issues are too complex for yes/no, true/false binary answers. Listen to those who have thought about the answers and might have looked at them from different angles.

2/12
Affinity bias: we like people who are like us. So why don’t you put yourself up for election, rather than voting for someone you’d like to have a beer with?

1/10
